newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan clothes makers search for "the Look".
newsitem.headline: Japan clothes makers search for "the Look".

text.p: Japanese clothing makers which once dressed the nation's women are losing ground to foreign labels which have "the look" that young women want to spend their money on.
A decade ago it was the "in" thing to buy a skirt at Cabin or a dress at Suzuya but changing tastes and a flood of foreign labels are making it hard for Japan's clothing retailers to stay in style.

"Large domestic retailers offer a vast choice of reasonably priced clothes without really emphasising a certain 'look'," said Seizo Mae, public relations manager at Renown Inc, Japan's largest apparel maker.
"Consumers nowadays don't just want something to wear, they want some sort of identity and our foreign competitors are ahead of us in creating such an element," he said.
In the 1980s "bubble economy" years, when consumers had money to burn, clothes makers expanded in all directions -- more shops, more styles, more frills, more expensive clothes.
When the bubble burst and purse strings got tighter, retailers switched to selling inexpensive clothes.
But they ended up in a vicious circle as they had to sell a greater volume to make ends meet, and that meant increasing their outlets even more.
Industry officials estimate the market share of domestic apparel retailers has fallen by about nine percent since the peak in 1991.
The decline has taken a heavy toll on onetime trend-setters like Suzuya, which recently went bankrupt with debts of 58.7 billion yen ($469 million). Other retailers are scaling back to survive.
Suzutan Co Ltd, Japan's largest retailer of women's clothes, plans to shut 150 of its 589 outlets by the end of February 1998 and Cabin Co Ltd aims to close 70 of its 396 shops by next February.

Cabin has forecast a parent net loss of 2.17 billion yen ($17.3 million) for the year to February 1997, which would be the fourth successive year of such losses. The results for the business year which just ended are due out shortly.
While Japanese retailers battle to return to profitability, foreign brands are strengthening their grip on the market.

"During the bubble-economy period, Japanese consumers came into contact with high-quality, overseas brand names which were a cut above mass-produced, domestic items," said Yutaka Hatano, marketing division manager at Donna Karan Japan KK. "They are finding the habit very hard to break."
In the year to December 1996, sales posted by the Japanese arm of Donna Karan International Inc totalled 28 billion yen ($224 million), a double-digit rise in percentage terms from the previous year.
Hatano attributed the success to the quality of the designs and the fact the clothes were only slightly more expensive to buy here than in the United States.
"Everything is designed in New York and targetted at the world. We do not re-design our garments to match Japanese tastes, and people like the originality," he said.
Industry analysts believe that Japanese retailers need to cut back their outlets more aggressively and become more responsive to what buyers want.
"Something is trendy when only a few people have that particular item and everyone wants one just like it," said Ari Sudo, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre.
"The industry has been neglecting consumer needs for too long, we must become more aware of the competitors and what the consumers want," said a Cabin official.
Renown, whose rehabilitation efforts started ahead of the others in 1994, is starting to reap the benefits.
Its sales rose for the first time since 1994 in the year to January 31, totalling 192 billion yen ($1.53 billion). ($1=125 yen)
